home.title: Find what's changing on Earth, where, and if it's real.
home.lead: Earth Trend Detective turns years of NASA satellite and model data into clear answers. Pick a variable, see where it is rising or falling across Mexico, and learn whether the change is real or just natural ups and downs.
home.showText: Maps by state, time series with a trend line, and a plain-language verdict. Every number comes with its units, period and source.
home.useText: Spot drier or wetter regions, sunnier skies, changing air quality or ozone. Useful for students, teachers, planners and curious people.
home.goalText: Make trend analysis honest and easy. We test every change with two statistical methods and say "no clear trend" when the data cannot tell.
home.step1: Pick what to study: rain, sunlight, soil moisture, runoff or air gases.
home.step2: States are colored by how fast the variable changes each decade. Hover to see details.
home.step3: The chart and verdict tell you if the change is real, how big it is, and how sure we are.
home.step4: Test your own eye in the Detective challenge before the data reveals the answer.
home.varsIntro: A variable is one thing NASA measures about our planet, such as how much rain falls or how much ozone sits above us. Choose one to see how it changed over four decades and where. Start with whatever you are curious about: water, sunlight or the air we breathe.
home.aux: Hover a side card or use the arrows to change variable. On touch screens, swipe.
home.challengeTitle: Think you can read the data?
home.challengeText: Before the numbers appear, we show you a variable and a region. You guess: rising, falling or no clear trend? Then we reveal what 40 years of NASA data say and why. Six quick cases that train your eye for real change versus natural noise.
home.howIntro: Four suggested steps, in order, to get the most out of the tool: start with the big picture on the map and finish by checking whether the change is real. You can jump around, but this route is the easiest way in.

precipitation.name: Precipitation
precipitation.def: Rain and snow reaching the ground, in millimetres per day. It decides where water is available and where floods or droughts may grow.
precipitation.what: All water that falls from the sky: rain, drizzle, snow and hail.
precipitation.shows: Average daily precipitation for each month and year, from the MERRA-2 model corrected with observations.
precipitation.read: Teal states are getting less rain, brown ones more. Faint colors mean the change could be chance.
precipitation.why: Water for crops, cities and rivers depends on it.

solar_radiation.name: Solar radiation
solar_radiation.alt: Sun with rays over the horizon
solar_radiation.def: Sunlight reaching the ground under real skies, in kWh per square metre per day. It drives temperature, plant growth and solar power.
solar_radiation.what: The energy from the Sun that actually arrives at the surface after clouds and haze.
solar_radiation.shows: Average daily sunlight per month and year, estimated from CERES satellite measurements.
solar_radiation.read: Purple states are getting less sunlight, orange ones more. Faint colors mean the change could be chance.
solar_radiation.why: It affects solar energy, evaporation and crop yields.

soil_moisture.name: Soil moisture
soil_moisture.def: How wet the top layer of soil is, from 0 (dry) to 1 (saturated). It tells plants and farmers how much water they can reach.
soil_moisture.what: The share of water held in the first centimetres of soil.
soil_moisture.shows: Surface soil wetness as a fraction between 0 and 1, from the MERRA-2 land model.
soil_moisture.read: Teal states are drying, brown ones are getting wetter. Faint colors mean the change could be chance.
soil_moisture.why: Dry soil signals drought risk and stress on crops.

surface_runoff.name: Surface runoff
surface_runoff.alt: Stream of water flowing over land
surface_runoff.def: Water that flows over the land instead of soaking in, in millimetres per day. It feeds rivers and can cause floods and erosion.
surface_runoff.what: The part of rain that runs along the surface towards streams and rivers.
surface_runoff.shows: Average daily runoff per month and year. Demo data for now: synthetic until the GLDAS ingestion runs.
surface_runoff.read: Teal states have less runoff, brown ones more. Faint colors mean the change could be chance.
surface_runoff.why: More runoff means more flood and erosion risk, less means less recharge.

no2.name: Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)
no2.def: A polluting gas from traffic, industry and fires, measured as a column of air. It is a clear marker of air quality in cities.
no2.what: The amount of NO₂ in the air column above each place.
no2.shows: Monthly average NO₂ column. Demo data for now: synthetic until the OMI ingestion runs.
no2.read: Blue states are getting cleaner, red ones more polluted. Faint colors mean the change could be chance.
no2.why: It harms lungs and helps form smog and acid rain.

ozone.name: Total ozone (O₃)
ozone.def: All the ozone in the column of air above us, in Dobson units. The ozone layer blocks harmful ultraviolet light.
ozone.what: The thickness of the ozone layer above each place.
ozone.shows: Monthly total ozone column in Dobson units, from the MERRA-2 reanalysis.
ozone.read: Blue states have less ozone, red ones more. Faint colors mean the change could be chance.
ozone.why: A thinner layer lets more ultraviolet light reach people and crops.

chart.title: How it changed over time
chart.subtitle: {{name}} in {{place}}: each dot is one {{unit}}, shown as {{kind}}.
chart.kindAnomaly: the difference from the usual value
chart.anomaliesTip: How far each point is above or below what is usual for that time of year. Removing the seasons makes real, long-term change easier to see.
chart.absoluteTip: The measured values as they are, including the seasonal ups and downs.
chart.legendSeriesTip: What the satellites and models measured.
chart.legendTrendTip: The steady rate of change that best summarises the data. It is robust to unusual years.
chart.legendRangeTip: The trend line should fall inside this band 95 times out of 100.

state.sumRising: {{name}} is rising by {{rate}} per decade. This is unlikely to be chance.
state.sumFalling: {{name}} is falling by {{rate}} per decade. This is unlikely to be chance.
state.sumNone: We can't tell a real change from natural variation (p = {{p}}). Try a longer period.
state.sumInsufficient: There isn't enough data to test a trend.
state.needMore: Widen the period to at least 10 years or pick a region with more data.

glossary.p: How likely a trend this strong is by pure chance. Below 0.05 is called significant.
glossary.sen: The median rate of change across all pairs of points. It resists outliers.
glossary.anomaly: A value minus the typical value for that calendar month.
glossary.ci: The range where the true rate of change probably lies, with 95% confidence.

detective.title: Detective challenge
detective.introLead: Real data hides real stories. Can you spot them before the numbers do?
detective.i1: We show you one variable and one region of Mexico.
detective.i2: You guess: is it rising, falling, or is there no clear trend?
detective.i3: We reveal what the NASA data say, with the rate of change and how sure we are.
detective.i4: Six cases, one per variable. Your score shows how well you read nature's signals.
detective.introNote: Tip: "no clear trend" is a valid answer. Sometimes the honest conclusion is that we cannot tell.

place.subtitle: See all six variables for one location.
place.outside: This tool covers Mexico. Showing the nearest grid cell.

info.title: More information
info.lead: How the app turns raw satellite data into an honest answer, in plain language.
info.s1: We subtract the typical value of each calendar month. What is left is an anomaly, so summer rain does not look like a trend.
info.s2: The Mann-Kendall test asks if values tend to go up or down over time, without assuming a straight line. It gives a p-value.
info.s3: Sen's slope is the median of all pairwise slopes. It gives the change per decade and is hard to fool with unusual years.
info.s4: A second opinion: a straight-line fit with a t-test and a 95% confidence band. If both methods agree, we say so.
info.s5: A map tests many states at once, so a few would look significant by luck. The Benjamini-Hochberg correction removes those false alarms.
info.readUp: The change is very unlikely to be chance and the variable is going up.
info.readDown: The change is very unlikely to be chance and the variable is going down.
info.readNone: We cannot tell a real change from natural variation. This is not the same as "no change".
info.readNot: Fewer than 10 years, or more than 30% of the data missing. We refuse to guess.
info.r1: p ≥ 0.05 is always "No clear trend", never "no change".
info.r2: Every number shows units, period and source.
info.r3: Color shows direction on the map, never good or bad.
info.validation: The team compares slope and p-value of sample series against NASA Giovanni and KNMI Climate Explorer. Results are kept in the repository.
info.src1: NASA POWER (MERRA-2 and CERES): precipitation, solar radiation, soil moisture, ozone.
info.src2: NASA GLDAS and OMI through Earthdata and Giovanni: runoff and NO₂ (pending, shown as demo data).
